c.tagline: Ancient walled river city of Teochew cuisine, gongfu tea and the floating Guangji Bridge.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis are cheap — most cross-town rides run ¥20–30. Didi is the main ride-hail app. Almost everything is paid via Alipay or WeChat Pay QR codes (both now accept linked foreign cards); carry a little cash as backup since Western credit cards are rarely swiped.

emergency.note: 110 is police, 120 is the ambulance/medical line, and 119 reaches the fire brigade.

hood_desc: The walled historic core, threaded by Paifang Street with its 22 restored stone memorial archways and by Jiadi Alley's Qing-era mansions; a warren of teahouses, snack stalls, ceramics shops and boutique inns — the must-stay heart for first-time visitors.

The eastern edge of the old town along the Han River, anchored by the Ming city wall, the Guangji (Xiangzi) Gate and the famous Guangji Bridge, a Song-dynasty span whose central section is a row of floating boats; scenic and photogenic, especially at dusk.

The northwest quarter around the 1,000-year-old Kaiyuan Temple and the willow-lined West Lake park; a calm, central area mixing temples, gardens and everyday local streets, walkable to all the sights.

The modern downtown around Chaozhou People's Square and its musical fountain, with malls, chain hotels, the city museum and wide avenues; the practical, convenient base with the most shopping and dining variety.

A quieter district southwest of the centre that is the engine of Chaozhou's world-famous ceramics industry, lined with porcelain factories, showrooms and workshops; local and low-key, good for buyers and browsers.

water.note: As across mainland China, drink boiled or bottled water rather than from the tap.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to around 9–10:00 PM; after that, taxis and Didi are the way to get around.
transit.note: The compact old city is best explored on foot — most sights are within walking distance. Buses reach outer districts and the high-speed Chaoshan railway station (about 45 minutes); taxis are cheap for longer hops.
transit.pay: Bus fares (from ¥2) are paid by scanning an Alipay/WeChat Pay QR code, tapping a transit card, or dropping exact cash in the farebox. There is no metro; buses and taxis/Didi cover the city.

landmarks: Guangji Bridge (Xiangzi Bridge)
One of China's four great ancient bridges spans the Han River on stone piers linked by a swinging pontoon of wooden boats, dismantled daily for ships.
Kaiyuan Temple
Founded in 738 during the Tang dynasty, this serene working monastery preserves exquisite courtyards, ancient stone pagodas, and masterworks of Chaozhou wood carving.
Paifang Street (Memorial Archway Street)
Twenty-plus rebuilt stone paifang arches honoring imperial scholars stride down the old town's main street, lined with teahouses and beef-ball vendors.
Guangji Gate Tower and Ancient City Wall
A majestic triple-eaved Ming gate tower anchors the restored riverside city wall, whose ramparts offer strolls overlooking Guangji Bridge and the Han River.
Hanwen Gong Temple (Han Yu Memorial Temple)
China's oldest surviving temple to Tang statesman-writer Han Yu climbs a forested hillside across the river, honoring the exile who transformed Chaozhou.
Chaozhou West Lake (Xihu Park)
A classical lakeside garden beneath Hulu Hill, where pavilions, moon bridges, and inscribed cliffs have inspired local poets since the Tang dynasty.
Jiadi Lane (Jiadixiang)
The old town's most refined lane preserves ornate Ming and Qing merchant courtyard mansions dripping with plasterwork, inscribed lintels, and nanyang nostalgia.
Phoenix Pagoda (Fenghuang Ta)
This seven-story Ming dynasty brick-and-stone pagoda of 1585 rises at a bend of the Han River, long the feng-shui guardian of Chaozhou.
Xu Fuma Mansion (Prince Consort Xu's Residence)
A rare Song dynasty aristocratic residence, nearly a millennium old, whose austere timber halls showcase China's finest surviving early domestic architecture.
Phoenix Mountain (Fenghuang Shan) Tea Country
A day trip into mist-wrapped mountains where centuries-old dancong tea trees produce Phoenix oolong, sipped gongfu-style in the villages that invented it.

train.note: Chaozhou has no international trains. Most arrivals use Chaoshan Station on the Xiamen-Shenzhen high-speed line, which serves both Chaozhou and Shantou - Xiamen is about 1.5 hours, Shenzhen about 2 hours and Guangzhou about 3 hours, and a city bus from the north exit takes around 45 minutes into the old town for ¥5. The older Chaozhou station in the north of the city handles conventional and some regional services. Book on 12306 with your passport and allow for the long transfer from Chaoshan when timing connections.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Chaozhou. Frequent buses run from Shantou (about ¥18-19, roughly an hour) including services from the China Travel Services station, and long-distance coaches connect Chaozhou with Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Xiamen from the city bus terminal. Tickets are bought at the counter or on Chinese apps; for Hong Kong or Macau you need to change to a cross-border coach in Shenzhen or Guangzhou.

ferry.note: Chaozhou sits inland on the Han River and has no scheduled passenger ferries - only small local craft and sightseeing boats near the Guangji Bridge. The nearest seaport is Shantou, about an hour away, and its former passenger sailings to Hong Kong no longer operate.

half.name: Nan'ao Island
half.blurb: A coastal island off Shantou reached via a scenic bridge, known for beaches, a lighthouse and a long seaside driving loop.

half.name: Shantou
half.blurb: A former treaty port with a colonial-era waterfront quarter, Xiaogongyuan, and a busy harbor distinct from Chaozhou's old town.
